US Army Fans AI:
The Blackbird Vanishes

Somewhere at NASA's Armstrong Flight Research Center in California, an empty patch of concrete is raising a lot of questions. The SR-71 Blackbird that sat on display there, tail number 844, the very last Blackbird ever built and the last one to fly, is gone. Satellite images show it vanished from its spot sometime before mid-May 2026, and NASA will only say it has "no additional information to share."

That silence has set the aviation world buzzing, because of what NASA's leadership has been saying elsewhere. In September 2026, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman unveiled a mysterious high-speed aircraft concept under the banner "rebuilding our X-plane portfolio" and declared that NASA was "getting back in the business of flying high and fast again." Asked point-blank whether the image was a Blackbird, he only smiled and said, "You sure that's a Blackbird?"

According to Aviation Week, which broke much of the story, the jet was moved into a hangar for inspection earlier this year, and NASA has reportedly reached out to former members of the SR-71 program about helping with a possible return to flight. NASA has not confirmed any of that, and no funding for such an effort has turned up in public budgets.

If it were true, it would be one of the most remarkable comebacks in aviation history. The SR-71 first flew in 1964 and still holds records that have stood for half a century. It cruised above 85,000 feet at more than three times the speed of sound, fast enough that its standard defense against enemy missiles was simply to accelerate and outrun them. No SR-71 was ever lost to enemy fire. The fleet was retired in 1998, and NASA flew its last two until 1999.

For now, the empty display stand is all anyone can confirm. But a lot of people who love this airplane are allowing themselves to wonder.

The U.S. Marine Corps is set to deploy one of its newest weapons to a remote Japanese island that sits just about 70 miles from Taiwan. During the joint U.S.-Japan exercise Keen Sword, running October 19 to 29, 2026, Marines will field the NMESIS anti-ship missile system on Yonaguni, Japan's southwesternmost inhabited island.

NMESIS, the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System, is a ground-based launcher that can hit ships at a range of roughly 115 miles. Fielded by the 12th Marine Littoral Regiment out of Okinawa, it is built for exactly this kind of mission: small, mobile teams spread across scattered islands, able to threaten enemy warships and then move before they can be found.

The drill is a large one. Around 45,000 Japanese troops are taking part, alongside forces from nine countries including Australia and France, while the U.S. Army deploys its own HIMARS launchers to nearby Ishigaki Island. The concept on display is distributed sea-denial, holding vital waterways at risk with mobile missile teams rather than relying on carriers alone.

The location carries weight. Yonaguni lies at the edge of a strategic chain of islands, and in 2022 Chinese ballistic missiles splashed down about 50 miles from it. Chinese commentators have criticized the deployment.

First Steps on Solid Ground

For the roughly 4,500 sailors and Marines aboard the aircraft carrier USS George H.W. Bush, this weekend brought something they had not seen in a long time: dry land. The carrier, along with the destroyer USS Delbert D. Black, pulled into Phuket, Thailand on October 4, 2026, for a port call and some well-earned shore leave.

It was the strike group's first port stop since leaving Naval Station Norfolk, Virginia, back in March, a stretch of about 7 months at sea that included a long deployment to the Middle East. "Our crew has performed exceptionally while underway, demonstrating discipline, resilience and unity," said the carrier's commanding officer, Capt. Justin T. Issler.

The visit makes the Bush the second U.S. carrier to call on Thailand in two months, following the USS Abraham Lincoln in September.

321 Days

The USS Abraham Lincoln left San Diego last November expecting a routine run through the Pacific. It came home this week after 321 days, nearly 11 months, one of the longest continuous deployments the Navy has seen in years. Somewhere along the way, the routine cruise turned into something else entirely.

Instead of the Pacific, the carrier and its strike group were sent to the Middle East. What followed was 40 days of sustained combat operations: 3,693 combat sorties flown by the aircrews of Carrier Air Wing 9, 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles launched, 77 one-way attack drones brought down, and a maritime blockade to help enforce. Through all of it, not one member of the strike group was lost to enemy action.

On October 7, with the ship back off San Diego and a day from pulling in, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth came aboard to pin a rare distinction on the group: the Presidential Unit Citation, one of the highest honors an entire unit can earn, and one the military hands out sparingly. It covers everyone in the fight, from the flight deck of the Lincoln to the escorts screening her, including the destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr.

Hegseth's main message to the crew wasn't about the operations at all. It was a request: thank your families for the months they spent waiting.

Then the Lincoln came home.

Just before noon on Thursday, the USS Abraham Lincoln slid up to the pier at Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, water cannons arcing over her flight deck and helicopters circling overhead. Hundreds of families crowded the waterfront, shouting and waving, many of them meeting sailors and Marines they had not seen in the better part of a year.

They had waited a long time. The Lincoln pulled out of San Diego last November for what was supposed to be a routine Pacific cruise. It became anything but. 

Redirected to the Middle East and handed two separate extensions, the carrier ended up away from home for 322 days, close to 11 months, with more than 200 of those days spent in a combat zone. At one stretch she went 286 straight days without a single port call, which the Navy considers a modern-day record.

What the crew did out there earned the strike group the Presidential Unit Citation, pinned on the day before they pulled in. But the number that mattered most on the pier was simpler. “Every sailor and Marine who deployed is returning,” said the carrier’s commanding officer, Capt. Daniel Keeler, who called the crew’s performance legendary. The ship came home with no lives lost, no aircraft lost, and no combat damage.

For the families, it was enough that the ship was finally tied up and the ramp was coming down. “They are all heroes,” said Carla Smith, whose son serves aboard the Lincoln, as she waited for him to step ashore.

Restocking a Proven Shield

When Iranian ballistic missiles streaked toward Israel in 2024, two U.S. Navy destroyers, the USS Arleigh Burke and the USS Carney, answered with the SM-3. It was the first time the interceptor had ever been fired in combat, and it worked. Now the Pentagon is paying to make sure it never runs short of them.

This week, Raytheon announced a five-year contract worth $6.3 billion, with two more option years, to keep its production line turning out the Standard Missile-3 Block IB. The deal is aimed squarely at one problem: America has been firing expensive interceptors faster than it can build them.

The SM-3 is an unusual weapon. It carries no explosive warhead. Instead, it destroys an incoming ballistic missile by slamming into it at tremendous speed, a technique known as hit-to-kill, essentially stopping a bullet with another bullet. Launched from both ships and land, and guided by an infrared seeker, it is built to catch enemy missiles in the middle of their flight, high above the earth.

The urgency is real. A recent think-tank report listed the SM-3 among seven critical munitions, alongside the Patriot, THAAD, and the Tomahawk, that U.S. forces are burning through faster than the stockpile can handle. “It has proven its relevance in combat,” said Raytheon president Phil Jasper, describing the interceptor as central to protecting U.S. forces and allies.

Building a weapon that works is one thing. Making sure you have enough of it is another, and that is what this deal is really about.

France is preparing to put Ukrainian pilots in the cockpit of one of Europe's most advanced fighter jets. The country's armed forces minister, Catherine Vautrin, told French lawmakers on October 8, 2026, that training of Ukrainian pilots on the Rafale will begin next month.

"From November, we will begin the first training of Ukrainian pilots on Rafale," Vautrin said.

The Rafale, built by France's Dassault Aviation, is a twin-engine multirole fighter and one of the most capable combat aircraft in European service, able to carry the long-range Meteor air-to-air missile among other munitions. The training is tied to a larger arrangement: Ukraine has agreed to eventually buy the jets, with a roadmap set in July for an initial batch of 16 Rafales and their weapons, part of a letter of intent for as many as 100.

Actual Rafales are not expected over Ukraine for a few years. French President Emmanuel Macron said earlier this year that the first could arrive around 2028 or 2029, which makes the November training an early first step. Ukraine's air force already flies F-16s supplied by several European countries and French Mirage 2000s.

Vautrin framed the move in broader terms for France. "We are fully aware that by supporting Ukraine, we are defending Europe," she told lawmakers.

The Most Exclusive Club in Aviation

There is a club you cannot buy your way into, cannot be invited to, and cannot apply for. The only way to become a member is to have your life saved by a Martin-Baker ejection seat. If that happens, the British company sends you a certificate, a patch, a pin, and a distinctive tie. It’s called the Ejection Tie Club, it was founded in 1957, and it has more than 6,000 members around the world.

Every one of them was, at some point, a pilot in an aircraft that was about to kill them.

That’s the job the ejection seat does, and it does it with staggering violence. In the span of a couple of seconds, a rocket-powered charge blasts the pilot and seat clear of the cockpit, punches them up and away from the doomed aircraft, and deploys a parachute, all while the body endures crushing G-forces that can briefly compress a pilot’s spine. It is brutal. It is also, very often, the difference between a funeral and a reunion.

The engineering has only gotten better. Since 1961, Martin-Baker’s seats have had what’s called “zero-zero” capability, meaning they can save a pilot even at zero altitude and zero speed, sitting still on the runway or tumbling just above the ground, situations that were once a death sentence.

The results speak for themselves. Martin-Baker says its seats have saved 7,827 lives since the first live test in 1945, and the number ticks up a little every year. The company now supplies ejection seats to 93 air forces across the globe.

7,827 pilots who should have died in a burning aircraft instead walked away, went home to their families, and got a tie in the mail.

Here's a math problem the U.S. Navy has been losing. An enemy sends a cheap drone, sometimes just a few thousand dollars' worth of parts, straight at a warship. The ship shoots it down with a surface-to-air missile that costs 1 to 2 million dollars each. The ship wins the fight and still loses, because the enemy can build drones faster and cheaper than the Navy can fire missiles at them.

The fix is deliberately low-tech and smart: a bigger cannon. It's called the Mk 38 Mod 4, built around the 30mm Mk 44 Bushmaster II, and it's now being fitted to Navy warships. It's the first time in more than 30 years the Navy has stepped up the size of this gun family, going from 25mm to 30mm, and it can fire airburst rounds that detonate right next to a drone and tear it apart. Each round costs a tiny fraction of a missile.

It's not just a bigger barrel. Each mount carries 400 rounds, pairs with a stabilized sight that has thermal imaging and a laser rangefinder, and links into the ship's Aegis combat system so it can be slewed onto a target automatically. The destroyer USS Mustin was the first warship to get it, fitted with two of the mounts, and test-fired it in the South China Sea in April.

And the Navy is scaling it up fast. It just expanded the program, with orders now totaling 55 mounts and deliveries running into 2031. The goal is to give warships a cheap, close-in layer of defense so the expensive missiles are saved for the threats that truly need them, like incoming cruise and ballistic missiles. A $25 cannon shell doing the job a $2 million missile used to do is exactly the kind of trade the Navy wants to be making.

Drones have rewritten the rules of naval warfare in just a few years, and the side that can defend itself without going broke is the side that stays in the fight. A 30mm cannon will never be glamorous. But in an age of swarms, cheap and reliable may matter more than flashy, and the Navy clearly agrees.

For decades the American way of war was built around a small number of very expensive machines: a few exquisite jets, a few high-end systems, each one a masterpiece and each one irreplaceable if it was lost. The Pentagon just signaled that era is ending, and the number it put on the table is staggering.

Speaking at the Association of the United States Army's annual meeting in Washington on October 14, 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the Pentagon is seeking roughly 50 billion dollars, as a one-time investment, to mass-produce drones and other autonomous systems. The goal he laid out is a change in scale that's hard to picture: taking the U.S. stockpile of autonomous systems from thousands of units to millions.

Hegseth said the department expects to handle "hundreds of thousands of one-way attack systems this year and into the millions in years to come." To get there, he argued the military has to stop thinking only in terms of a few costly platforms and start buying cheap systems it can build at enormous scale, the kind of math that has reshaped the battlefield in recent conflicts, where swarms of inexpensive drones have gone up against billion-dollar equipment.

Just as important as the money is who gets to build it. Hegseth pushed to open the door to new, smaller companies in a market long dominated by a handful of giant traditional contractors, while still valuing those established firms. He also called for cutting the red tape that slows production down, telling his officials bluntly, "I want you to tell me which rules can be signed away."

This isn't starting from zero. Late last year the Army kicked off its own one-billion-dollar "Drone Dominance" effort to buy around 340,000 small drones for combat units over two years, with tens of thousands expected to reach soldiers in 2026 and hundreds of thousands by 2027. The 50-billion-dollar request still has to clear Congress, so none of it is guaranteed. But the direction is unmistakable: the most powerful military on earth has decided its next edge isn't one perfect machine, it's a million cheap ones.

Think about this for a second. The newest B-52 in the Air Force was built in 1962. The oldest crews flying it today weren't born yet when it was already old. And the Air Force has no plans to retire it, in fact, it intends to keep the B-52 in the air into the 2050s. By then the plane will have served for roughly 100 years.

The B-52 Stratofortress first flew in 1952 and entered service in 1955. Boeing built the last one, an H model, in 1962, and the H is the only version still flying today, about 76 of them. Every single one is older than the parents of the young airmen who fly them. No other combat aircraft in history has come close to that kind of run.

So why does it refuse to die? Because nothing has ever matched what it does for the price. The B-52 can haul an enormous load over intercontinental distances, carry almost every weapon in the inventory, and do it cheaply compared to newer jets. Rather than replace it, the Air Force is rebuilding it: new Rolls-Royce F130 engines to replace the originals, a modern radar, and upgraded electronics. The rebuilt aircraft gets a new name, the B-52J, and a new lease on life that stretches for decades.

That endurance has created something you almost never see in aviation. Take the family of Col. Don Sprague, who flew every B-52 model from the A all the way to the H and commanded the 23rd Bomb Squadron at Minot Air Force Base in the early 1970s. Decades later his grandson, Capt. Daniel Welch, became a B-52 aircraft commander in that very same squadron, with Daniel's father having flown the B-52 in between. Three generations of one family, all on the same plane.

And here's the part that stops people cold: because the B-52 is on track to fly for a full century, a pilot climbing into one today could be strapping into the exact same airframe his grandfather flew, and someday his own grandson might fly it too. There is no other machine of war on earth you can say that about. The B-52 was built to outlast the Cold War. It ended up outlasting almost everyone who ever doubted it, and it still has decades left to go.

For 45 years, when American soldiers needed to get somewhere fast, the Black Hawk helicopter carried them. The Army just picked its successor, and the strange thing about it is that it isn't really a helicopter at all. It takes off straight up like one, then tilts its rotors forward and flies like an airplane.

It's called the MV-75 Cheyenne II, built by Bell, and it won the Army's competition to replace a large part of the Black Hawk fleet. The trick is the tiltrotor design: two big rotors sit on the wingtips and point straight up for takeoff and landing, then rotate forward in flight so the aircraft cruises on its wings like a plane. That's what lets it beat a conventional helicopter on both speed and distance.

The numbers are a real jump. The MV-75 is designed to fly at more than 300 miles per hour, carry up to 14 soldiers, and sling an external load of up to 10,000 pounds. Bell says it has over double the speed and range of the aircraft it replaces. That reach is the whole point: the Army has the vast distances of the Pacific in mind, where getting troops across hundreds of miles of ocean quickly is the hard part.

Soldiers helped shape it. The Army's 101st Combat Aviation Brigade at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, the first unit set to receive the aircraft, gave feedback that drove real design choices, down to the seating layout and leaving the cockpit without doors. The Army has also pulled the timeline forward: the first aircraft are now expected in 2027, years ahead of the original target, and the service could field up to 334 of them by 2040.

It isn't in service yet. Bell's current contract covers a handful of test aircraft, and the funding still has to clear Congress like everything else in the budget. Bell's own people call it "revolutionary," which is the kind of thing a maker says about its own product. But strip out the sales pitch and the core fact stands on its own: after nearly half a century, the Army is moving past the helicopter for its assault fleet, toward something that flies twice as far and nearly twice as fast.

For years, the Gray Eagle has been one of the Army's quiet workhorses, a long-endurance drone, a cousin of the famous Reaper, that can stay in the air for most of a day to watch, scout, and strike. Now there's a new version of it, and for the first time, the National Guard is getting its own.

It's called the Gray Eagle 25M, and the "M" stands for "modernized." Built by General Atomics, it first flew in December 2023 under a 389 million dollar contract. On the outside it looks much like the Gray Eagle troops already know, but the important changes are under the skin.

The 25M was rebuilt around an open architecture, which means it can be upgraded and reconfigured far faster than before, along with advanced datalinks and a new propulsion system. The payoff: it carries more, flies longer, and is far harder for an enemy to jam. That last part matters most. On today's battlefield, both sides are constantly trying to blind and scramble each other's drones with electronic attack, so a drone that can keep flying and keep its link when someone's trying to cut it off is exactly what the Army wants.

The milestone is who's getting it. The Arizona Army National Guard will be the first state to stand up a full unit flying the Gray Eagle 25M, receiving 8 aircraft by September 2027 and 4 more by the end of 2029, for 12 in all. It's the start of something bigger: Congress has funded three of these Guard units, and the Guard wants a drone company in each of its eight infantry divisions. In other words, citizen-soldiers are about to be operating genuinely front-line drone technology.

The pedigree is real. General Atomics says the Gray Eagle family has logged more than 1 million hours of flight, with automatic takeoff and landing built in. Putting a modernized, jam-resistant version of it in the hands of the National Guard says a lot about where warfare is going, drones aren't just for the active-duty force overseas anymore. They're becoming a core tool for the troops who defend the homeland, too.

American soldiers are back on the far eastern edge of NATO. A new rotation of troops from the U.S. Army's storied 1st Infantry Division, the "Big Red One," has begun arriving in Lithuania, a small Baltic nation that sits on the border with Russia's Kaliningrad territory and with Belarus.

As of mid-October, about 100 soldiers were on the ground at the Pabrade training area, with more flowing in over the following weeks. Lithuania's defense minister, Robertas Kaunas, said the troops are arriving in batches and that two full battalions are expected to be in place by mid-November. The Pentagon first announced the deployment back in August.

It's a rotational mission, meaning units cycle in and out rather than setting up a permanent home, and its purpose is straightforward: reassure a nervous ally and deter any Russian move against NATO's eastern flank. Lithuania has been one of the loudest voices for a steady American presence. It has gone so far as to offer to pay the cost of building a permanent U.S. base on its own soil.

The backdrop is the unease that has gripped the Baltic states since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Those three small countries, once part of the Soviet Union, know better than most what it means to share a border with Moscow, and American boots on their ground have become a powerful symbol of the promise at the heart of NATO: an attack on one is an attack on all.

For a country of fewer than 3 million people living in the shadow of a far larger neighbor, the sight of U.S. soldiers training in the forests near the frontier is reassurance that lands in a way no treaty on paper can. It's the quiet, visible side of an alliance, show up, stand alongside your partners, and make clear that no one on the line is standing there alone.

The commanding officer of the USS George Washington says Iranian attempts to strike ships near the Strait of Hormuz have been unsuccessful.

Speaking to reporters on October 20, Capt. Nicholas DeLeo said Iran had tried to strike "a variety of ships" in the area. "Those have all been unsuccessful, and I can tell you that reason is 100% due to our sailors on this ship," he said.

He did not specify which ships were targeted. The account comes from the Navy and has not been independently verified.

The carrier is operating in the Arabian Sea, supporting the US blockade of Iran and providing cover for commercial ships moving through the Strait of Hormuz. In September, the Navy confirmed Iran had attempted to hit US warships with ballistic missiles.

Separately, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to the region this week. Axios reported he met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The Pentagon declined to comment on the reports.

In 2009, Dakota Meyer drove straight into an ambush in Afghanistan's Ganjgal Valley, again and again, to pull out wounded men and recover the fallen. His actions were credited with saving 13 Americans and 23 Afghan troops, and in 2011 he received the Medal of Honor, the nation's highest award for valor. Now the Marine has been handed a very different kind of mission: making sure the troops who serve today have a decent place to sleep at night.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has named Meyer a senior advisor to the Pentagon's Barracks Task Force. The job is simple and hands-on. Meyer will travel the country, base to base, walking through barracks, talking with the service members who live in them, and flagging what needs to be fixed. His first stops are in California this week, Camp Pendleton, then Twentynine Palms and Miramar, and if the schedule holds he'll have inspected around 21 bases by the end of December.

The problem he's being sent to tackle is real and long-running. Government watchdogs have reported for years that many enlisted troops live in substandard barracks, some with serious health and safety issues. An August 2026 report put the military's installation maintenance backlog at an estimated 285 billion dollars. Hegseth has called the living conditions "unacceptable," and the task force, formed in late 2025, is meant to set department-wide standards and steer money toward the worst of it.

Some of that money is already moving. A major 2025 defense funding law set aside roughly 1.2 billion dollars for barracks improvements, including a dedicated Marine Corps "Barracks 2030" effort and funds to restore and modernize housing across the Army, Navy, Air Force, and Space Force. Recent projects include new and modernized housing at bases in Georgia and Washington state.

What makes this one land is who's carrying it, and why. Meyer knows exactly what these troops give, because he gave it himself. "They shouldn't have to fight for basic living conditions when they come home at night," he said. And he's putting his own name on the outcome: "If we don't get this fixed, there's only one person to blame. Me." For the men and women living in those rooms, having a Medal of Honor Marine show up in person to see the state of them is about as strong a signal as the Pentagon can send that someone is finally paying attention.

Most countries don't offer to pay for someone else's military base. Poland is doing exactly that. It has been pushing hard for a permanent U.S. base on its territory, and it has put billions of its own dollars on the table to make it happen.

Poland formally requested a new permanent American base in June 2026, and the talks have moved quickly since. Polish President Karol Nawrocki has gone as far as calling the base "confirmed," and U.S. officials have said there's been "major progress." That said, Washington has not announced a final decision, and no location has been named yet, so the deal isn't signed, it's close, according to the Polish side.

The part that stands out is who pays. Poland has signaled it is willing to cover much of the cost itself. Polish officials have put their share at more than 15 billion zloty, roughly 3.4 billion euros, and a Bloomberg report placed the figure as high as 4.4 billion dollars. For a country that sits directly on the border with Russia's Kaliningrad territory and with Belarus, a permanent American presence is clearly worth paying for.

The base would likely house a full brigade, somewhere between 3,000 and 5,000 U.S. troops, with Poland's deputy defense minister calling 4,500 the most realistic number. Over time, Poland would like to see as many as 15,000 American troops in the country. Right now, roughly 6,500 to 7,000 rotate through on a non-permanent basis.

Plenty is still undecided, the exact location, the final cost split, even the name (Poland's president has floated calling it "Fort Trump"). But the direction is clear, and it's unusual. In a long-running debate about whether America's allies pay their fair share, Poland isn't asking the U.S. to spend more. It's offering to spend its own money to keep American troops close.

RAF Fairford, in the English countryside, is one of the forward bases the U.S. Air Force leans on most, a launch point for American heavy bombers operating over Europe and the Middle East. Earlier this month, the U.S. quietly pulled every one of its B-1B Lancer bombers out of it. All 12 were flown home, and the reason given was security: a threat serious enough to move a bomber force off a base it had been using for active operations.

The trigger appears to trace back to the morning of September 27, when police were called to three suspicious vans parked near the base, in the village of Whelford. Dozens of homes were evacuated while armed officers and bomb-disposal teams moved in. In the end, no explosive devices were found, though investigators did recover a quantity of gasoline. Five British men in their 20s were arrested on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses. Two more arrests followed, bringing the total to seven. All were released on bail.

Then it escalated. On October 20, two men from London were rearrested, this time under the UK's National Security Act, on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service. Police identified them as a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian national. No one has been charged with anything yet, and the five other men remain on bail. But the senior officer on the case, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said police "consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement." The investigation is ongoing.

The American response had already come. On October 4, roughly a week after the incident, the U.S. withdrew all 12 of its B-1B Lancers from Fairford, citing new threats. President Trump confirmed that a threat drove the decision to move them. The base matters in this story for a specific reason: it had hosted U.S. aircraft involved in strikes tied to the confrontation with Iran earlier in 2026, which is exactly the kind of history that puts a target on a place.

It's worth being careful here, this is an open investigation, no charges have been filed, and the full picture isn't public yet. But the shape of it is already striking. The standoff with Iran didn't end when the bombs stopped falling. It appears to have followed the aircraft home, to the gates of a quiet base in Gloucestershire, and it was enough to make the U.S. decide its bombers were safer somewhere else.

Line up a row of Navy fighters and they all look more or less the same, grey on grey, built to disappear against the sky. So for decades, one aircraft stopped everybody who walked past it: a single F-14 Tomcat painted glossy black from nose to tail, with a white Playboy bunny sitting right on the fin. It had a name, "Vandy 1," and most people just called it the Black Bunny.

The jet belonged to VX-4, "The Evaluators," the Navy's Air Test and Evaluation Squadron based at Point Mugu, California. These were the people who wrung out new missiles, radars, and systems before the fleet ever saw them. By long tradition, the squadron commander's personal aircraft flew under the call sign "Vandy 1," short for "Vanderbilt 1," and it was always the black one, painted that way on purpose so there was no mistaking whose jet it was.

The bunny came first, and it came with a story. Navy squadrons had been putting rabbits on their tails since the 1950s, but VX-4 made it famous. The black bunny scheme started back in 1969 on an F-4 Phantom used for night testing. Then in 1971, Playboy's lawyers noticed, and the company warned the Navy it might take legal action over the logo. Instead of a fight, they struck a deal: Playboy backed off and actually supplied the squadron an official bunny stencil, so the Navy could keep painting it the right way. No lawsuit, just a handshake and a stencil.

The bunny moved onto the Tomcat in 1985, when two F-14As were assigned to the squadron and given the black treatment. By 1990 the Black Bunnies were flying F-14As in permanent gloss black, and the jet became a genuine flight-line celebrity, the one everybody wanted a photo of, the one that looked like it had wandered in from a movie set.

It couldn't last. In 1994, VX-4 merged with another test squadron to form VX-9, and the bunny quietly disappeared from the Tomcats. But the Navy gave it one last ride: the very last F-14 ever built was painted up as the Black Bunny for its farewell flights before being parked as a gate guardian. Today the livery is gone, but the legend isn't. In an age of grey airplanes designed to be invisible, somebody once flew a jet-black Tomcat with a bunny on the tail, and dared you not to look.

Readiness isn't a one-time action; it's a constant state of mind.

For a U.S. Army Warfighter, readiness means being prepared to execute any mission, anywhere, at any time. Aboard this CH-47 Chinook, Sgt. Jesus Escudero isn’t just a passenger. As a helicopter repairer and aircrew member, he conducts meticulous in-flight checks.

U.S. Army photo by Spc. Thomas Nguyen

On the morning of March 27, 2026, the "Alarm Red" siren went off at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia. An Iranian attack was inbound. Staff Sgt. Kalob Mitchell, Sgt. Xavier Jones, and Spc. Nicholas Cabo did what they'd trained to do and moved to cover inside Bunker 100. Then a 550-pound Iranian ballistic missile struck near them. The blast threw all three into an interior wall and knocked them out. "Everything went black," Mitchell said. "We'd been hit."

Mitchell came to first. He checked on Jones and Cabo, and then he heard it: screaming from the other side of the bunker. What the three of them did next is why they're being honored. Dazed and injured themselves, they went straight to the wounded. They put tourniquets on a severely hurt soldier and worked to keep him alive. They treated another man with a neck injury and calmed a third who was disoriented from the blast. Jones and Cabo loaded a wounded soldier onto a stretcher and carried him out to an ambulance. Cabo did all of it while bleeding from a wound in his own leg, and stayed on his feet to keep helping.

The three serve with the 6th Battalion, 56th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, part of the 1st Cavalry Division Artillery, the air defenders whose whole job is to stand between incoming fire and the people on the ground. The strike came during Operation Epic Fury, the confrontation with Iran that began earlier in 2026. That day, the thing they train to stop got through, and they met it the only way left to them: by saving the people next to them.

On October 1, at the III Armored Corps headquarters at Fort Hood, Texas, Mitchell, Jones, and Cabo each received the Purple Heart. Their commander, Capt. Tyler Ritter, read aloud from thank-you notes sent in after the attack. One of them was short and said everything: "Sir, your soldiers saved my life." Lt. Gen. Kevin D. Admiral, who leads III Armored Corps, pointed to the three of them as what readiness and grit actually look like when it counts.

They've been honest about the cost, too. The recovery has been hard, trouble sleeping, anxiety in crowds, and repeated hospital stays that took them from Germany to Virginia and finally home to Fort Hood. And they've used the attention to tell other soldiers something that matters: be straight with the medics, and don't be too proud to ask for help putting yourself back together. "We did our job to the best of our ability," Mitchell said, "and we almost paid the ultimate price." They didn't. They paid in blood, kept their heads, and carried their brothers out. That's the whole story, and it's enough.

The Marine Corps has stood up its first medium missile battalion.

On October 9, 1st Battalion, 10th Marine Regiment, 2nd Marine Division, at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina, was converted from an artillery battalion into the Corps' first battalion dedicated to land-based anti-ship missiles.

The unit will operate NMESIS, the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System. It's a remotely operated launcher that carries two Naval Strike Missiles, which the Marine Corps says have an effective range of more than 130 nautical miles against ships and fixed targets on land.

NMESIS was first fielded to the 3rd Marine Littoral Regiment in Hawaii in 2024. The Marine Corps says the system is meant to complement its cannon artillery, not replace it, and 10th Marines will keep artillery in another battalion.

Here's something most people never think about: nearly every large-caliber barrel for the U.S. Army's howitzers and tank cannons comes from one place. The Watervliet Arsenal in upstate New York, which first opened during the War of 1812, is the only plant that makes them, and it's showing its age. Now the Pentagon has a problem it can't ignore: that single arsenal can't keep up with demand, so on October 22 the Army put out a public call for new manufacturers to help build the barrels.

What changed is Ukraine. The war has burned through artillery at a rate the modern U.S. hadn't planned for. A barrel isn't forever, every round fired wears it down, and after enough shots it has to be replaced. A Pentagon budget document noted that Ukraine's heavy use of the M777 howitzer alone created demand for more than 30 replacement barrels a month, on top of the broader push across America and Europe to produce more ammunition and refill stockpiles that the war had drawn down.

The Army's notice spells out what it's looking for, with responses due November 23. It wants a supplier that can build up to 10 barrels a month within three years, show it can make 155mm barrels within 18 months, and price out an initial run of 40 cannon tubes. It even specifies the ability to coat steel tubes up to 30 feet long and 7,500 pounds. In plain terms: the Army wants a second source, so the whole supply doesn't hang on one aging building.

This is the unglamorous side of military power, the industrial base. It's easy to focus on the howitzer itself, but a cannon is only as useful as a country's ability to keep feeding it fresh barrels and ammunition. For decades, one arsenal was enough. A single hard war on the other side of the world showed that it isn't anymore. The Army is also weighing bigger changes, including whether to eventually replace the towed M777 with a system based on South Korea's K9.

None of this makes headlines the way a new jet does, but it's exactly the kind of quiet limit that decides how long a military can actually fight. You can field the best artillery in the world, but if the barrels wear out faster than one old plant can build them, that's a real ceiling.

On October 15, on a training range at Fort Knox, Kentucky, the U.S. military tried something that sounds like science fiction and isn't. At U.S. European Command's request, DARPA sent out a team of four self-driving robots to hunt for enemy positions on their own. The whole point was to test an idea the Pentagon is taking seriously: sending machines into a fight ahead of human soldiers. Fort Knox was chosen because its terrain can stand in for a European battlefield.

Here's how it played out. An operator received satellite imagery of a suspected enemy position and pointed the robotic team at it. One vehicle rolled forward alone, using its own sensors to search, and when it spotted a likely position, it stopped and waited for orders. Two more robots moved up to support it, and a simulated rocket struck the target about 300 yards away. The lead vehicle even carried a drone it could launch to scout ahead or strike. The machines can also haul supplies and ammunition, or carry wounded soldiers out.

One part matters more than anything else, and the military was clear about it: the robots drive and spot targets on their own, but a human still makes the decision to fire. As DARPA technical adviser Jason Gregory put it, the systems handle the moving and the detecting, but "they don't pull the trigger until a human says pull the trigger." The autonomy is in getting there and finding the enemy, not in deciding to use force.

The reason behind all of this sits on NATO's eastern edge. The effort is part of what's called the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, and the concept is blunt: a force of robots, drones, and sensors that would absorb the first blow if a NATO country were invaded, soaking up the opening hits so that human troops don't have to. It is aimed squarely at the possibility of a Russian move against the alliance, and it draws directly on lessons from Ukraine, where cheap drones and unmanned systems have rewritten how wars are fought. The idea was championed by recently retired Gen. Christopher Donahue.

It's still early. Right now the robots can drive themselves, scout, and wait for orders, and the next round of testing in December will put real soldiers alongside them to see how it actually works. No one is replacing troops with machines. But the direction is clear, and a little startling: the United States is seriously preparing for a day when the first thing an invading army runs into on NATO's frontier isn't a soldier, but a robot built to take the hit in a soldier's place.

Something happened over the Mediterranean last week that had never happened before. On October 20 and 21, France and the United Kingdom flew their first-ever joint airborne nuclear-strike exercise, codenamed "Rummy." Royal Air Force Eurofighter Typhoons escorted French Rafale jets on a simulated nuclear-strike mission out of Saint-Dizier air base in eastern France. No actual warheads were involved, it was a rehearsal, but the fact that it happened at all is the story.

To understand why it matters, you have to know how fiercely independent France has always been about its nuclear forces. Its Strategic Air Forces have operated alone since the 1960s, answering to Paris and no one else. One analyst called flying a nuclear mission alongside another country a "revolution." It grows out of the Northwood Declaration, signed in July 2025, in which France and Britain agreed to coordinate their nuclear forces and declared there is no extreme threat to Europe that wouldn't draw a response from both of them.

Here's why Americans should care. This is happening because Europe is nervous. With open questions about how reliable the U.S. nuclear umbrella will be in the years ahead, and a Russia that keeps rattling its own arsenal next door, Europe's only two nuclear powers are quietly building a backup. France calls the broader idea "forward deterrence." In plain terms, two of America's closest allies are rehearsing how to protect the continent with or without Washington.

They're careful to say they aren't merging their forces. "Having independent nuclear forces doesn't exclude coordination," said French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin. Both countries keep their own weapons and their own launch decisions, which they do not share. France brings something Britain doesn't have, an airborne leg, with Rafales that carry nuclear-tipped cruise missiles; the UK's deterrent rides entirely on submarines. So this exercise paired France's air-launched punch with British jets flying guard.

For most of the last 80 years, the security of Western Europe has rested, ultimately, on the American guarantee. Two allies rehearsing a nuclear strike together, without the U.S. in the cockpit, is a quiet but real signal that they are preparing to stand on their own if they ever have to. Whether you find that reassuring or unsettling depends on where you sit. Either way, it's a shift worth watching, because it says as much about trust in America as it does about France and Britain.

Teamwork Makes the Boom Work

A perfectly coordinated crew is the key to effective artillery. Cannon crewmembers from the 4th Infantry Division work in sync to operate the M777 Howitzer during training.

📷 Army Sgt. Charlyn Abuyo

Aerial refueling sounds impossible until you realize the US military does it thousands of times a year: two aircraft flying just a few feet apart, both at over 300 mph, five miles up, passing fuel through a rigid boom. It's routinely called one of the most demanding tasks in all of aviation, and it's the quiet backbone of American airpower, the thing that lets fighters cross oceans and bombers stay up for a full day.

On the Air Force's newest tanker, the KC-46, the boom operator doesn't even lie in the tail anymore; they do it remotely, by camera and 3D screen. And now the Air Force wants to add AI, software that would watch each refueling through the tanker's cameras and give crews an objective debrief afterward, to cut mistakes and train them faster.

To be clear, it's an analysis and training tool, not AI flying the plane, a human still controls the boom. One of aviation's oldest and hardest skills is about to get a very modern assistant.

There's a spacecraft the United States has been flying since 2010 that most people have never heard of, and that's partly the point. It's called the X-37B. It looks like a miniature version of the old Space Shuttle, about 29 feet long, but there's no crew aboard. It launches straight up on a rocket, spends months or even years in orbit doing things the government mostly won't talk about, then glides back down and lands itself on a runway, no pilot required.

Built by Boeing and now operated by the U.S. Space Force, the X-37B has flown eight missions over roughly 15 years, designated OTV-1 through OTV-8. It has ridden to space on a range of rockets, from the Atlas V to SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy. And unlike most spacecraft, it comes home and flies again, which is exactly what makes it valuable: a reusable test bed the military can send up, recover, and reuse.

What really sets it apart is endurance. These aren't quick trips. One mission, OTV-6, stayed in orbit for 908 days, roughly two and a half years, before coming home, a record for the program. The most recent flight, OTV-8, launched in 2025 on a Falcon 9. The spaceplane can simply loiter up there, running its experiments, for as long as the mission calls for.

Officially, the X-37B is a platform for testing next-generation space technology. Over the years it has carried experiments on how materials and seeds hold up to space radiation, a Naval Research Laboratory experiment on beaming solar power, and it has released small satellites. On a more recent flight it tested "aerobraking," using the faint drag of the upper atmosphere to change its orbit while saving fuel. But the specific payloads are usually secret, and that secrecy fuels endless speculation about what else it might be doing, inspecting other satellites, testing surveillance gear, or simply keeping adversaries guessing. The Space Force's line is consistent: it's a test platform.

And honestly, the mystery is part of the capability. Space is becoming a contested domain, and having a reusable, maneuverable spacecraft that can stay up for years, carry classified experiments, change its orbit, and then land to fly again is a serious tool, and a quiet signal. Whatever exactly the X-37B is doing on any given mission, its very existence says the United States intends to be very comfortable operating in orbit for a long time to come.

For years, hypersonic weapons have been the rarest and most expensive things in the American arsenal, a handful of exquisite, hand-built systems that cost a fortune per shot. A three-year-old startup is trying to flip that completely. On October 8, a company called Castelion, founded by former SpaceX engineers, posted a photo of its new hypersonic, named Blackbeard, streaking out of a launcher mounted on the back of a mobility truck. Their slogan for the image said it all: "Built to move with the fight."

The big idea isn't that Blackbeard is faster than other hypersonics. It's that it's cheap. Castelion wants to build these at scale and at low cost, so that a hypersonic can be treated less like a national treasure and more like ordinary ammunition, something you can fire freely instead of rationing. The Army's target is to get roughly 80 percent of the capability of its planned next-generation precision missile at a fraction of the cost per round.

That's a genuine break from how the U.S. has done this. The Army's other hypersonic, the Dark Eagle, is powerful but relies on large, specialized, expensive launch equipment. Blackbeard is designed to fire from the kind of mobile launchers the Army already uses, like the fire-control system behind HIMARS, and the ground-launched version is a compact two-stage design with a maneuvering payload. Castelion has hinted at a range of just under 500 miles, though it hasn't released full performance numbers.

And the military is backing it with real money. The Navy is already working to fit Blackbeard onto the F/A-18 Super Hornet, flew a developmental test with the missiles under a jet in September, and put down a 105 million dollar contract earlier this year. The Pentagon has signaled that once testing is done, it plans a multi-year deal for at least 500 missiles a year, and it's seeking the funding to buy more than 12,000 over five years. A production-representative Army launch is planned for 2027.

None of this is proven yet, the hardest tests are still ahead, and the real-world performance of the production version is still under wraps. But the direction is what matters. For a long time, America's answer to hypersonics was a small number of incredibly expensive ones. Blackbeard is a bet that the better answer is thousands of cheap ones you can fire off the back of a truck. If it works, it doesn't just add a new weapon, it changes the math of a fight. That's why a company barely three years old suddenly has the full attention of the Pentagon.

There are few images more sacred to the United States military than the flag-raising on Iwo Jima, six men hauling the Stars and Stripes up a pole on Mount Suribachi in February 1945, frozen forever in Joe Rosenthal's photograph. A stone version of that moment stands near the National Museum of the Marine Corps, just outside the gates of Quantico. This week, a man walked up to it with a sledgehammer.

On October 21, in Triangle, Virginia, police got a call about someone vandalizing the memorial. When officers arrived, they found a 27-year-old man attacking the limestone statue and took him into custody without incident. By the time he was stopped, he had knocked the head clean off one of the figures and done enough other damage that the repair bill is expected to run into the hundreds of thousands of dollars. He has been charged with felony destruction of property and injury to a monument, and is being held without bond. Police have not offered a motive.

To understand why this stings the way it does, you have to understand what the statue means. It's a smaller version of the Marine Corps War Memorial sculpted by Felix de Weldon, the bronze original that was dedicated in Arlington on the Marine Corps' birthday in 1954. The site near Quantico isn't just a roadside landmark. It's where Marines hold promotions, commissionings, retirements, and reenlistments. For generations of Marines, some of the proudest moments of their careers happened standing in front of that flag.

And the men it depicts were real. The figure believed to have been struck is Cpl. Harlon Block, who helped raise that flag and was killed in action on Iwo Jima just days later, one of nearly 7,000 Americans who gave their lives taking that small volcanic island. The statue was never really about the stone. It's about them.

The museum's director, Keil Gentry, says the repairs will be challenging, and experts are already being consulted. The statue will be rebuilt, the head restored, the damage undone. But a memorial's power was never in the material. You can take a sledgehammer to the figure of Harlon Block. You cannot touch what he and the others did on that mountain, or the reverence the Corps still holds for it. That outlasts any act of vandalism, and it always will.

खड्की काठमाडौं–६ का दुई कार्यकाल क्षेत्रीय सभापति भइसकेका नेता हुन्। उनी गगन थापाका पूर्वशिक्षकसमेत हुन्। सामान्यतया राठौर र थापाबीच मुख्य प्रतिस्पर्धा हुने अनुमान गरिए पनि खड्कीको उम्मेदवारी कायम रहेपछि कांग्रेसको सभापति चुनाव थप रोचक बनेको छ।

अमेरिकाको प्रतिनिधिसभामा H-1B Visa Fraud Crackdown Act (H.R. 10643) नामक नयाँ विधेयक दर्ता भएको छ। विधेयक पारित भए गम्भीर एच–१बी नियम उल्लंघन गर्ने रोजगारदातामाथि २ लाख ५० हजार अमेरिकी डलरसम्म जरिवाना र केही अवस्थामा कम्तीमा १० वर्षसम्म एच–१बी प्रायोजनमा प्रतिबन्ध लगाउन सकिने प्रस्ताव गरिएको छ।

रिपब्लिकन सांसद बेथ भान डुयनसहित ६ जना सांसदले अक्टोबर १ मा दर्ता गराएको विधेयक मुख्यतः रोजगारदाता र एच–१बी कार्यक्रमको दुरुपयोगलाई लक्षित गरिएको छ। अमेरिकी कामदार विस्थापित हुने गरी जानाजानी नियम उल्लंघन गरेमा सबैभन्दा कडा कारबाहीको प्रस्ताव गरिएको छ।

विधेयकमा इमिग्रेसनसम्बन्धी कागजातमा ठगी गरेमा समेत १० हजारदेखि ५० हजार डलरसम्म जरिवाना बढाउने प्रस्ताव छ। तर यसले हालको एच–१बी भिसाको संख्या, योग्यता वा आवेदन शुल्कमा प्रत्यक्ष परिवर्तन गर्ने प्रस्ताव भने राखेको छैन।

विधेयक हाल हाउस जुडिसियरी कमिटीमा विचाराधीन छ। पारित भएर राष्ट्रपति समक्ष पुगेपछि मात्र कानुनी रूपमा लागू हुने प्रक्रिया अघि बढ्नेछ।

रुस–युक्रेन युद्धपछि प्रभावित नेपाली नागरिकको सुरक्षा र स्वदेश फिर्ताका लागि नेपालले कूटनीतिक पहल जारी राख्दै आएको छ। नेपालले रुस र युक्रेन दुवैसँग समन्वय गरी नेपालीको उद्धार तथा फिर्तीका लागि प्रयास गरिरहेको जनाएको छ।

यसअघि मे महिनामा तत्कालीन परराष्ट्रमन्त्री शिशिर खनालले युक्रेनी विदेशमन्त्री एन्ड्री सिबिहासँग नौ जना नेपाली युद्धबन्दीलाई मानवीय आधारमा रिहा गरी नेपाल फर्काउन आग्रह गरेका थिए।

यस्तै, रुसी सेनामा कार्यरत अवस्थामा ज्यान गुमाएका नेपालीका परिवारलाई क्षतिपूर्ति उपलब्ध गराउने प्रक्रिया पनि अघि बढिरहेको छ। पछिल्लो छलफललाई युद्धबाट प्रभावित नेपालीको अवस्था समाधान तथा स्वदेश फिर्ती प्रयासलाई थप प्रभावकारी बनाउने कूटनीतिक पहलका रूपमा हेरिएको छ।

टरिगाउँलाई वैकल्पिक विमानस्थल बनाउने तयारी, मन्त्रीसहित प्राविधिक टोली स्थलगत अध्ययनमा

तुलसीपुरस्थित टरिगाउँ विमानस्थल स्तरोन्नति र धावनमार्ग विस्तारका लागि सरकारले प्रक्रिया अघि बढाएको छ। संस्कृति, पर्यटन तथा नागरिक उड्डयनमन्त्री खड्गराज पौडेल ‘गनेस’सहित मन्त्रालय र नेपाल नागरिक उड्डयन प्राधिकरणका प्राविधिक टोलीले बुधबार विमानस्थलको स्थलगत अध्ययन गरेका छन्।

सरकारले चालु आर्थिक वर्षमा विमानस्थल विकासका लागि २५ करोड रुपैयाँ बजेट विनियोजन गरेको छ। ७२ सिटे विमान नियमित सञ्चालन गर्न सक्ने गरी विमानस्थललाई स्तरोन्नति गर्ने लक्ष्य राखिएको छ।

मन्त्री पौडेलले नेपालगन्ज विमानस्थलमा प्रतिकूल अवस्था आए टरिगाउँलाई वैकल्पिक विमानस्थलका रूपमा प्रयोग गर्न सकिने बताएका छन्। प्रारम्भिक प्राविधिक सुझावमा धावनमार्गको क्षमता सकारात्मक देखिएको भन्दै विस्तृत अध्ययनपछि आवश्यक काम अघि बढाइने उनले बताए।

नेपाल नागरिक उड्डयन प्राधिकरणका महानिर्देशक मुकेश डंगोलले विमानस्थलको सुरक्षालाई पहिलो प्राथमिकता दिँदै कम लागतमा स्तरोन्नति गर्ने उपाय खोजिने बताए। ७२ सिटे विमान अवतरणको प्राविधिक सम्भावनाबारे विस्तृत अध्ययनपछि निष्कर्षमा पुगिने उनले बताए।

२०११ सालमा स्थापना भएको टरिगाउँ विमानस्थल लामो समयदेखि पूर्ण क्षमतामा सञ्चालन हुन सकेको छैन। छोटो धावनमार्गका कारण ठूला विमान सञ्चालनमा समस्या रहँदै आएको अवस्थामा यसपटक बजेटसहित स्तरोन्नतिको काम अघि बढाउने तयारीले स्थानीयमा नयाँ आशा जगाएको छ।

दुर्घटनामा घाइते बचाउन दौडिने अब डराउन नपर्ने! उद्धारकर्तालाई कानुनी संरक्षण दिने विधेयक

सरकारले सडक दुर्घटनापछि घाइतेको उद्धार तथा उपचारमा जुट्ने व्यक्तिलाई कानुनी संरक्षण दिने व्यवस्थासहित राष्ट्रिय सडक सुरक्षा विधेयक, २०८३ प्रतिनिधिसभामा दर्ता गरेको छ।

विधेयकअनुसार दुर्घटनालगत्तै घाइतेलाई प्राथमिक उपचार गर्ने वा अस्पताल पुर्‍याउने व्यक्तिले असल नियतले काम गर्दा थप क्षति वा मृत्यु भए पनि देवानी वा फौजदारी कारबाहीको भागीदार बन्नुपर्ने छैन। त्यस्तै, सरकारी वा गैरसरकारी स्वास्थ्य संस्थाले घाइतेको तत्काल उपचार सुरु गर्नुपर्ने व्यवस्था प्रस्ताव गरिएको छ।

लोकमार्गका सहरी क्षेत्रमा ट्रमा सेन्टर, निश्चित दूरीमा एम्बुलेन्स सेवा र घाइते उपचारका लागि ‘एकद्वार प्रणाली’ लागू गर्ने प्रस्ताव पनि विधेयकमा छ। सार्वजनिक सडक निर्माण, डिजाइन तथा रुट परमिटअघि अनिवार्य रोड सेफ्टी अडिट गर्नुपर्ने व्यवस्था गरिएको छ।

जोखिमपूर्ण सडकमा सुधार नभएसम्म यातायात सेवा रोक्न सिफारिस गर्न सक्ने राष्ट्रिय सडक सुरक्षा परिषद् गठन गर्ने प्रस्ताव गरिएको छ। परिषद्ले सवारी साधनका आधारभूत सुरक्षा मापदण्ड र हेलमेटको गुणस्तरसमेत निर्धारण गर्नेछ।

त्यस्तै, पहिचान नखुलेका सवारीबाट हुने हिट एन्ड रन तथा बीमाविहीन दुर्घटनाका पीडितलाई परिषद्को कोषबाट क्षतिपूर्ति दिने व्यवस्था प्रस्ताव गरिएको छ। नेपाल प्रहरी, अस्पताल र बीमा कम्पनीलाई जोडेर एकीकृत डिजिटल ‘सडक दुर्घटना अभिलेख तथा घाइते उद्धार व्यवस्थापन प्रणाली’ सञ्चालन गर्ने योजना पनि विधेयकमा समेटिएको छ।

खोज तथा उद्धार अभियानका लागि हाइटेरा र अवडेलले सुरक्षा निकायलाई दियो करोडौंको सञ्चार उपकरण

विश्वव्यापी सञ्चार प्रविधि कम्पनी हाइटेरा र नेपालस्थित साझेदार अडेलले नेपाल प्रहरी र सशस्त्र प्रहरीलाई खोज तथा उद्धार एवं विपद् प्रतिकार्यका लागि करिब १० करोड रुपैयाँ बराबरका सञ्चार उपकरण सहयोग गरेका छन्।

हस्तान्तरण गरिएका उपकरणमा बडी–वर्न क्यामेरा, पुस–टु–टक ओभर सेलुलर रेडियो र ई–प्याक पोर्टेबल रिपिटर लगायत हार्डवेयर तथा सफ्टवेयर छन्। यी प्रविधिलाई एकीकृत गरी केन्द्रीय कमाण्ड सेन्टरमार्फत सञ्चार व्यवस्थापन गर्न सकिने बताइएको छ।

सामान्य सञ्चार नेटवर्क अवरुद्ध वा अनुपलब्ध हुँदा ई–प्याक रिपिटरले प्रभावित क्षेत्रमा अस्थायी रेडियो नेटवर्क स्थापना वा विस्तार गर्न सहयोग गर्नेछ। पुस–टु–टक रेडियोमार्फत सेलुलर नेटवर्क प्रयोग गरी समूहगत सञ्चार तथा स्थानसम्बन्धी सूचना आदानप्रदान गर्न सकिनेछ।

त्यस्तै, बडी–वर्न क्यामेराले सुरक्षाकर्मीको अडियो तथा भिडियो रेकर्ड गर्नुका साथै आवश्यक अवस्थामा कमाण्ड सेन्टरमा प्रत्यक्ष जानकारी पठाउन सक्नेछ। भूकम्प, बाढी, पहिरो, हिमाली उद्धारलगायत विपद्का समयमा यी उपकरण उपयोगी हुने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ।

प्रहरी महानिरीक्षक दानबहादुर कार्कीले सहयोगले सुरक्षा निकायलाई प्रविधिमैत्री बनाउन तथा दुर्गम क्षेत्रमा उद्धार र सञ्चारलाई प्रभावकारी बनाउन महत्वपूर्ण योगदान पुग्ने बताए। कम्पनीले नेपाली सेनालाई समेत सञ्चार उपकरण सहयोग गर्ने कार्यक्रम रहेको जनाएको छ।

मुस्ताङको शिन्ता मणि फेरि चम्कियो! विश्वप्रसिद्ध अवार्डमा एसियाका उत्कृष्ट होटलमध्ये तेस्रो

मुस्ताङको शिन्ता मणि मुस्ताङले २०२६ को Condé Nast Traveller Readers’ Choice Awards मा ‘Rest of Asia’ विधातर्फ तेस्रो स्थान हासिल गरेको छ। ९५.३७ अंक प्राप्त गरेको शिन्ता मणि यो वर्षको सूचीमा परेको नेपालका दुई होटलमध्ये एक हो।

यसै सूचीमा काठमाडौंको द्वारिकाज् होटल दोस्रो स्थानमा रहेको छ। उक्त अवार्ड Condé Nast Traveller का बेलायतका पाठकहरूले गरेको मतदानका आधारमा प्रदान गरिएको हो।

शिन्ता मणि मुस्ताङले मुस्ताङको प्राकृतिक भूगोल, स्थानीय वास्तुकला र संस्कृतिसँग जोडिएको आतिथ्यका साथै संस्कृति, वेलनेस, अन्वेषण र स्थानीय समुदायसँगको सम्बन्धमा आधारित अनुभव प्रदान गर्दै आएको छ।

होटलले स्थानीय रोजगारी, स्थानीय आपूर्तिकर्ता तथा समुदायसँगको सहकार्यलाई समेत प्राथमिकता दिँदै आएको बताइएको छ। यो अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय सम्मानले नेपाललाई अर्थपूर्ण र उच्चस्तरीय पर्यटन गन्तव्यका रूपमा विश्वमाझ चिनाउन थप योगदान पुग्ने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ।

गगनसँगै मैदानमा खड्की पनि! ‘उम्मेदवारी कायमै छ’ भन्दै श्यामकृष्णले दिए यस्तो स्पष्ट जवाफ

नेपाली कांग्रेसका नेता श्यामकृष्ण खड्कीले पार्टी सभापति पदमा आफ्नो उम्मेदवारी कायमै रहेको स्पष्ट पारेका छन्। अनलाइनखबरसँग कुरा गर्दै खड्कीले उम्मेदवारी फिर्ता लिनेबारे कुनै सहमति नभएको बताएका हुन्।

सभापति पदमा खड्कीसहित गगनकुमार थापाको उम्मेदवारी कायम छ। यसअघि उम्मेदवारी दिएका किशोरसिंह राठौरले भने उम्मेदवारी फिर्ता लिएका छन्।

खड्कीले आफूले उम्मेदवारी फिर्ता लिने विषयमा वार्ताको प्रस्ताव आएको तर त्यसलाई अस्वीकार गरेको बताए। उनले भने, ‘मलाई वार्तामा बसौं भनेर प्रस्ताव आएको हो। तर मैले मानिनँ। मेरो उम्मेदवारी कायमै छ, कायमै रहन्छ।’

कांग्रेसको नयाँ नेतृत्व चयनका लागि बिहीबार बिहान १० बजेदेखि मतदान हुँदैछ।

अस्ट्रेलियाबाट नेपाललाई फेरि ठूलो सहयोग! बाढी प्रभावितका लागि थप १५ मिलियन डलर घोषणा

अस्ट्रेलियाले हालैको बाढी तथा विपद्बाट प्रभावित नेपालका लागि थप १५ मिलियन अस्ट्रेलियन डलर सहयोग घोषणा गरेको छ। मेलबर्नमा परराष्ट्रमन्त्री शिशिर खनाल र अस्ट्रेलियाकी विदेशमन्त्री पेनी वङबीच भएको भेटवार्ताका क्रममा सहयोग घोषणा गरिएको हो।

यसअघि अस्ट्रेलियाले आपत्कालीन प्रतिकार्यका लागि प्रतिबद्ध गरेको ११ मिलियन अस्ट्रेलियन डलरमा नयाँ १५ मिलियन थपिएको हो। नयाँ सहयोग राहत, उद्धारपछि प्रारम्भिक पुनर्लाभ तथा पुनर्निर्माणका काममा केन्द्रित हुने जनाइएको छ।

भेटवार्तामा नेपाल–अस्ट्रेलिया सम्बन्ध थप सुदृढ बनाउने, जलवायु परिवर्तन, विपद् जोखिम न्यूनीकरण, पूर्वसूचना प्रणाली तथा जलवायु–उत्थानशील पूर्वाधारमा सहकार्य विस्तार गर्ने विषयमा छलफल भएको छ।

यस्तै, नेपालमा अस्ट्रेलियाबाट मान्यताप्राप्त टीभीईटी संस्था तथा विश्वविद्यालयका सम्भावित स्याटेलाइट क्याम्पस स्थापना गर्ने विषयमा पनि छलफल भएको छ। मन्त्री खनालले नेपाली विद्यार्थीका लागि न्यायोचित विद्यार्थी भिसा व्यवस्था गर्न आग्रह गरेका छन्।

दुवै देशबीच व्यापार, प्रत्यक्ष विदेशी लगानी, नवीकरणीय ऊर्जा, कृषि, पर्यटन, श्रम गतिशीलता तथा प्रत्यक्ष हवाई सम्पर्क विस्तार गर्ने विषयमा समेत छलफल भएको जनाइएको छ।

मोदीले मनाउँदै सार्वजनिक जीवनको २५ औं वर्षगाँठ, बालेन र रविले दिए शुभकामना

भारतीय प्रधानमन्त्री नरेन्द्र मोदीले सार्वजनिक जीवनमा २५ वर्ष पूरा गरेका छन्। उनले सन् २००१ अक्टोबर ७ मा गुजरातको मुख्यमन्त्रीका रूपमा शपथ लिएसँगै सुरु भएको राजनीतिक तथा प्रशासनिक यात्राको २५ वर्ष पूरा गरेका हुन्।

मोदी गुजरातको मुख्यमन्त्रीका रूपमा तीन कार्यकाल रहेपछि सन् २०१४ देखि भारतको प्रधानमन्त्री छन्। उनको २५ वर्षे सार्वजनिक सेवाको अवसरमा विभिन्न देशका नेताहरूले शुभकामना दिएका छन्।

यसै अवसरमा नेपालका प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाह (बालेन) र राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टीका सभापति रवि लामिछानेले पनि मोदीलाई शुभकामना दिएका छन्। बालेनले मोदीको समर्पित सार्वजनिक सेवाको प्रशंसा गर्दै आगामी दिनमा पनि सफलता र समृद्धिको शुभकामना दिएका छन्।

रविले मोदीको नेतृत्वमा भारतले गरेको रूपान्तरण र प्रगतिलाई प्रेरणादायी भन्दै नेपाल–भारतबीचको ऐतिहासिक, सांस्कृतिक तथा जनस्तरको सम्बन्धलाई अझ सुदृढ बनाउन सहकार्यको अपेक्षा व्यक्त गरेका छन्।

एआईजीदेखि चोलेन्द्रसम्म नेक्सस देखिएका इनमविरुद्ध सम्पत्ति शुद्धीकरणमा अनुसन्धान

पूर्वप्रधानन्यायाधीश चोलेन्द्र शमशेर जबरा र सशस्त्र प्रहरीका एआईजी वंशीराज दाहालसँग सम्बन्ध रहेको दाबी गरिएका इनम सापकोटाविरुद्ध सम्पत्ति शुद्धीकरणको कसुरमा अनुसन्धान अघि बढाइएको छ। काठमाडौं जिल्ला प्रहरी परिसरको हिरासतमा रहेका सापकोटामाथि बुधबारदेखि म्याद लिएर अनुसन्धान सुरु गरिएको जनाइएको छ।

काठमाडौं जिल्ला अदालतले सुरुमा एक दिनको म्याद दिएको थियो। म्याद सकिएपछि थप अनुसन्धानका लागि बिहीबार उनलाई पुनः अदालतमा उपस्थित गराइएको स्रोतले जनाएको छ।

सापकोटालाई यसअघि त्रिभुवन अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय विमानस्थलबाट पक्राउ गरिएको थियो। उनी विभिन्न व्यक्तिबीच सम्पर्क तथा ‘सेटिङ’ मिलाउने भूमिकामा रहेको दाबी गर्दै प्रहरीले अनुसन्धान अघि बढाएको बताइएको छ।

यसै प्रकरणसँग जोडेर एआईजी वंशीराज दाहाल निलम्बित भई छानबिनमा छन्। उनीमाथि अनुमति बिना संवेदनशील अवस्थामा रहेका व्यक्तिसँग भेटघाट गरेको र सुरक्षा सूचना चुहाएको आरोप लगाइएको छ।

यता, पूर्वप्रधानन्यायाधीश चोलेन्द्र जबराको निवास तथा उनका निकटस्थ र आफन्तका घरमा सम्पत्ति शुद्धीकरण अनुसन्धान विभागले छापा मारेर कागजात तथा सामग्री नियन्त्रणमा लिएको बताइएको छ।

तर सापकोटा, दाहाल वा जबरासँग जोडिएका यी आरोप तथा अनुसन्धानका विषय अदालतबाट प्रमाणित भइसकेका छैनन्। अनुसन्धानको निष्कर्षपछि मात्रै वास्तविक अवस्था स्पष्ट हुनेछ।

आवाजविहीनका आवाज बन्दै बिध्या चापागाईं, ‘हेर्ने कथा’ले जोड्यो १७ लाखभन्दा बढी दर्शक

पत्रकार तथा कथावाचक बिध्या चापागाईंले ‘हेर्ने कथा’मार्फत ओझेलमा परेका नेपालीका जीवन, संघर्ष र आशाका कथा विश्वसामु पुर्‍याउँदै आएकी छन्।

ग्रामीण तथा पहुँचबाट टाढा रहेका समुदायका वास्तविक कथा प्रस्तुत गर्दै आएको हेर्ने कथालाई अहिले १७ लाख १० हजारभन्दा बढी दर्शकले युट्युबमा फलो गरिरहेका छन्। उनका सामग्रीले सामान्य नागरिकका आवाजलाई देश–विदेशका दर्शकसम्म पुर्‍याएको छ।

बिध्याको कामले नेपाली समाजका अनसुना कथालाई सार्वजनिक बहस र अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय दर्शकसम्म पुर्‍याउने पुलको भूमिका खेलिरहेको छ। संघर्षरत मानिसका कथा प्रस्तुत गर्ने उनको शैलीले ठूलो समुदायलाई निरन्तर जोड्दै आएको छ।

चोलेन्द्रले जग भत्काए, प्रकाशमानले विधि खोजे, मनोजले आफूखुसी निर्णय लिए

सर्वोच्च अदालतमा संवैधानिक इजलास गठनको विषय फेरि विवादमा परेको छ। प्रधानन्यायाधीश डा. मनोजकुमार शर्माले बुधबार गठन गरेको इजलासमा न्यायाधीशहरूबीच मतभेद भएपछि संवैधानिक इजलास बस्न सकेन।

बुधबार प्रधानन्यायाधीश शर्मासहित सपना प्रधान मल्ल, हरिप्रसाद फुयाँल, नहकुल सुवेदी र अब्दुल अजिज मुसलमान रहेको इजलास तोकिएको थियो। न्यायाधीश फुयाँलले आफूलाई इजलासमा समावेश गर्ने आधारबारे प्रश्न उठाएपछि विवाद चर्किएको बताइएको छ।

संवैधानिक इजलास गठनको प्रक्रियाबारे लामो समयदेखि बहस हुँदै आएको छ। तत्कालीन प्रधानन्यायाधीश चोलेन्द्र शमशेर जबराको कार्यकालमा ‘पिक एन्ड चुज’को आरोप लागेपछि यो विषय झन् संवेदनशील बनेको थियो। त्यसपछि इजलास गठनमा पारदर्शिता र निश्चित मापदण्डको माग हुँदै आएको छ।

प्रधानन्यायाधीश प्रकाशमानसिंह राउतको कार्यकालमा पनि संवैधानिक इजलास गठनको विधि सुधार गर्ने विषयमा बहस भएको थियो। वरिष्ठताका आधारमा इजलास गठन गर्ने वा अन्य पारदर्शी विधि अपनाउने भन्नेमा स्पष्ट स्थायी अभ्यास बन्न नसक्दा विवाद दोहोरिँदै आएको देखिन्छ।

नेपालको संविधानको धारा १३७ अनुसार प्रधानन्यायाधीशको नेतृत्वमा संवैधानिक इजलास रहने र न्याय परिषद्को सिफारिसमा प्रधानन्यायाधीशले तोकेका अन्य चार न्यायाधीश सदस्य रहने व्यवस्था छ। तर चार न्यायाधीश छनोट गर्दा वरिष्ठतालगायत कुन विस्तृत मापदण्ड अपनाउने भन्ने विषयमा स्पष्टता नहुँदा प्रश्न उठ्ने गरेको छ।

संवैधानिक इजलासले संविधानसँग सम्बन्धित गम्भीर विवाद, संघ–प्रदेश तथा प्रदेश–स्थानीय तहबीचको अधिकार विवाद, निर्वाचन तथा अयोग्यतासम्बन्धी विषयलगायत मुद्दा हेर्ने भएकाले इजलास गठनको पारदर्शिता र विश्वसनीयता न्यायिक प्रक्रियाका लागि महत्वपूर्ण मानिन्छ।

त्रिविको वार्षिकोत्सवमै शिक्षामन्त्रीविरुद्ध प्रदर्शन! ‘नेपोबेबी’ भन्दै राजनीतिक हस्तक्षेप अन्त्य गर्न माग

त्रिभुवन विश्वविद्यालय (त्रिवि) को ६७औँ वार्षिकोत्सव कार्यक्रमका क्रममा शिक्षा तथा खेलकुदमन्त्री एवं त्रिविका सहकुलपति सस्मित पोखरेलविरुद्ध विद्यार्थी तथा युवाले प्रदर्शन गरेका छन्। मन्त्री पोखरेल वार्षिकोत्सव सभामा सहभागी हुन मुख्य क्याम्पस परिसर पुगेका बेला विद्यार्थीले विरोध जनाएका हुन्।

प्रदर्शनकारीले ‘नेपोबेबी’ र ‘मुर्दावाद’ लगायतका नारा लगाउँदै त्रिविमा हुने भनिएको राजनीतिक भागबन्डा, नियुक्ति तथा हस्तक्षेप अन्त्य गर्न माग गरेका थिए। विद्यार्थीले विश्वविद्यालयमा योग्यताका आधारमा नेतृत्व र नियुक्ति हुनुपर्ने भन्दै विरोध जनाएका हुन्।

त्रिवि सभाको बैठकमा मन्त्री पोखरेलले शैक्षिक क्यालेन्डर कार्यान्वयन, नतिजा समयमै प्रकाशन, अधिकार विकेन्द्रीकरण, डिजिटल प्रणाली र अनुसन्धानमा जोड दिनुपर्ने बताएका छन्। उनले विद्यार्थीको नतिजा एक महिनाभित्र सार्वजनिक गर्न निर्देशनसमेत दिएका छन्।

वार्षिकोत्सवकै दिन भएको प्रदर्शनले विश्वविद्यालय सञ्चालनमा राजनीतिक हस्तक्षेप र नियुक्तिको विषयमा विद्यार्थी असन्तुष्टि अझै कायम रहेको देखाएको छ।

सांसदलाई हराउँदै अर्जुन खनाल बने राप्रपा गण्डकीको अध्यक्ष, पञ्चराम गुरुङ पराजित

राष्ट्रिय प्रजातन्त्र पार्टी (राप्रपा) गण्डकी प्रदेशको अध्यक्षमा अर्जुन खनाल निर्वाचित भएका छन्। बिहीबार सम्पन्न निर्वाचनमा उनले निकटतम प्रतिस्पर्धी तथा गण्डकी प्रदेशसभा संसदीय दलका नेता पञ्चराम गुरुङलाई २५ मतले पराजित गरेका हुन्।

खनालले १८९ मत प्राप्त गर्दा गुरुङले १६४ मत पाए। ४२८ मतदाता रहेको निर्वाचनमा ३६० जनाले मतदान गरेका थिए भने ७ मत बदर भएको निर्वाचन समितिले जनाएको छ।

खनाल राप्रपाका केन्द्रीय सदस्य तथा पर्यटन विभागका सदस्य हुन्। उनी गत प्रतिनिधिसभा निर्वाचनमा कास्की–३ बाट उम्मेदवार बनेका थिए।

पञ्चराम गुरुङले गण्डकीमा चार वर्ष अध्यक्षको पहिलो कार्यकाल पूरा गरेपछि निर्वाचनमार्फत नेतृत्व हस्तान्तरण गरेका हुन्। ४१ सदस्यीय प्रदेश कार्यसमितिका सदस्यहरू भने सर्वसम्मत निर्वाचित भएका छन्।

कामदारलाई खुसीको खबर! अब हरेक वर्ष एक महिनाको आधारभूत तलब बराबर चाडपर्व भत्ता अनिवार्य

सरकारले सबै रोजगारदाता तथा प्रतिष्ठानलाई आफ्ना कामदारलाई अनिवार्य रूपमा चाडपर्व भत्ता उपलब्ध गराउन निर्देशन दिएको छ। श्रम ऐन, २०७४ को दफा ३७ अनुसार प्रत्येक कामदारले हरेक वर्ष एक महिनाको आधारभूत पारिश्रमिक बराबर रकम चाडपर्व भत्ताका रूपमा पाउने अधिकार रहेको छ।

कानुनअनुसार रोजगारदाताले तोकिएको चाडपर्व भत्ता उपलब्ध गराउनुपर्ने हुन्छ। कामदारले भत्ता नपाएमा आफ्नो कार्यक्षेत्र हेर्ने श्रम तथा रोजगार कार्यालय वा श्रम तथा व्यवसायजन्य सुरक्षा विभागमा उजुरी गर्न सक्ने व्यवस्था छ।

सरकारले श्रमिकको कानुनी अधिकार कार्यान्वयन गर्न रोजगारदाता र प्रतिष्ठानहरूलाई नियमअनुसार चाडपर्व भत्ता उपलब्ध गराउन आग्रह गरेको छ।

विश्वका संसद्मा नेपालको ठूलो जित! जलवायु विपद्सम्बन्धी प्रस्तावले पायो दुईतिहाइ बहुमत

तान्जानियाको अरुसामा जारी अन्तरसंसदीय संघ (आईपीयू) को १५३औँ महासभामा नेपालले प्रस्तुत गरेको जलवायुजन्य विपद्सम्बन्धी आपत्कालीन प्रस्ताव दुईतिहाइभन्दा बढी बहुमतले पारित भएको छ।

सभामुख डोलप्रसाद (डीपी) अर्यालले प्रस्तुत गरेको ‘हिमालयी क्षेत्र तथा अन्य जोखिमपूर्ण क्षेत्रमा जलवायु विपद्को सामना र उत्थानशीलता सुदृढ गर्ने संसदीय कदम’ शीर्षकको प्रस्तावको पक्षमा ९०१ मत, विपक्षमा ७८ मत परेको थियो भने १४० मत तटस्थ रहेको थियो।

सभामुख अर्यालले जलवायु परिवर्तनका कारण हिमालय, हिमनदी र हिमतालमा जोखिम बढिरहेको उल्लेख गर्दै जलवायु न्याय, विपद् पूर्वसूचना प्रणाली र अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय सहकार्य आवश्यक रहेकोमा जोड दिएका थिए।

प्रस्तावमा जलवायु तथा मौसमसम्बन्धी सीमापार पूर्वसूचना प्रणाली, प्रविधिमा पहुँच, विपद् जोखिम न्यूनीकरण र जलवायु प्रतिबद्धता कार्यान्वयनमा सरकारलाई संसदीय तहबाट जवाफदेही बनाउने विषय समेटिएका छन्।

प्रस्ताव पारित भएसँगै अब आईपीयू महासभामा जलवायु विपद्, हिमालय संरक्षण, वित्तीय तथा प्राविधिक सहयोग र जोखिमयुक्त क्षेत्रमा उत्थानशीलता बढाउने उपायबारे छलफल हुनेछ। यसलाई नेपालले जलवायु परिवर्तनका असरप्रति विश्वको ध्यानाकर्षण गराउने महत्वपूर्ण कूटनीतिक उपलब्धिका रूपमा हेरिएको छ।

दसैँ मनाउन गाउँ फर्किनेको लर्को! २४ घण्टामै ४९ हजारभन्दा बढीले छाडे काठमाडौं उपत्यका

दसैँ नजिकिएसँगै काठमाडौं उपत्यका छाडेर घर फर्किने यात्रुको संख्या बढ्न थालेको छ। काठमाडौं उपत्यका ट्राफिक प्रहरी कार्यालयका अनुसार असोज २१ गते एकै दिनमा ४९ हजार २६४ यात्रु उपत्यकाबाट बाहिरिएका छन्।

प्रहरीका अनुसार उक्त अवधिमा ७ हजार ६३१ वटा सवारीसाधन उपत्यकाबाट बाहिरिएका थिए। चाडपर्व नजिकिँदै गर्दा घर फर्किने यात्रु र बाहिरिने सवारीसाधनको चाप बढ्दै गएको छ।

दसैँ मनाउन आफ्नो गाउँघर फर्किने यात्रुको संख्या थप बढ्ने अनुमान गरिएको छ।

शिक्षकलाई गाडी किन्न सरकारले ८०% ब्याज अनुदान दिने प्रस्ताव! कसले कति मूल्यको गाडी किन्न पाउने?

सरकारले शिक्षकहरूलाई बैंकबाट ऋण लिएर सवारीसाधन खरिद गर्न सहज बनाउने उद्देश्यले किस्तामा लाग्ने ब्याजको ८० प्रतिशतसम्म अनुदान दिने प्रस्ताव अघि सारेको छ।

प्रस्तावअनुसार माध्यमिक तहका प्रथम श्रेणीका शिक्षकले अधिकतम ५० लाख रुपैयाँसम्म र द्वितीय श्रेणीका शिक्षकले ४० लाख रुपैयाँसम्मको सवारीसाधन खरिद गर्न पाउनेछन्। त्यस्तै, निम्नमाध्यमिक र प्राथमिक तहलगायतका योग्य शिक्षकले अधिकतम ४ लाख रुपैयाँसम्मका दुईपाङ्ग्रे सवारीसाधन खरिद गर्न सक्ने प्रस्ताव छ।

उक्त प्रस्ताव स्वीकृतिका लागि अर्थ मन्त्रालयमा पठाइएको छ। योजना स्वीकृत भएमा शिक्षक सेवामा बहाल रहँदासम्म मात्रै ब्याज अनुदान उपलब्ध हुने जनाइएको छ।

पोखरामा स्कुल बस भीरबाट खस्दा ४ विद्यार्थीसहित ५ जनाको मृत्यु, १४ जना घाइते

कास्कीको पोखरा महानगरपालिका–२८ माझथानामा शुक्रबार बिहान स्कुल बस दुर्घटना हुँदा चार विद्यार्थीसहित पाँच जनाको मृत्यु भएको छ भने १४ जना घाइते भएका छन्। कास्की प्रहरी प्रमुख एसपी नवीन कार्कीका अनुसार मृत्यु हुनेमा तीन छात्रा, एक छात्र र एक स्थानीय व्यक्ति छन्।

कालिका इङ्लिस बोर्डिङ स्कुलका विद्यार्थी बोकेर कालिकातर्फ आउँदै गरेको बस ओख्लेको भीरबाट करिब २०० मिटर तल खसेको थियो। दुर्घटनामा घाइते भएकाहरूलाई उद्धार गरी उपचारका लागि अस्पताल लगिएको छ।

प्रहरी, नेपाली सेना र स्थानीयवासी उद्धारमा खटिएका थिए। मृतकको पहिचान तथा दुर्घटनाको कारणबारे थप विवरण आउन बाँकी रहेको जनाइएको छ।

एआईजी वंशीराज दाहालले इनम सापकोटासँगको संवाद स्विकारे, छानबिन प्रतिवेदन गृह मन्त्रालयमा

पूर्वप्रधानन्यायाधीश चोलेन्द्र शमशेर जबरासँग सम्बन्धित घटनामा विवादमा आएका सशस्त्र प्रहरीका निलम्बित एआईजी वंशीराज दाहालले इनम सापकोटासँग मोबाइल र ह्वाट्सएपमा कुराकानी हुने गरेको स्वीकार गरेका छन्।

दाहालमाथि छानबिनको जिम्मेवारी पाएका एआईजी अन्जनीकुमार पोखरेलले अनुसन्धान पूरा गरी प्रतिवेदन गृह मन्त्रालयमा बुझाएका छन्। असोज १९ गते दाहाललाई निलम्बन गर्दै मन्त्रालयले छानबिन अघि बढाएको थियो।

छानबिनका क्रममा दाहालले झापाको चिनजानका आधारमा सापकोटासँग संवाद हुने गरेको बताएको स्रोतको भनाइ छ। यस्तै, प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाहको गतिविधि तथा लोकेसनसम्बन्धी संवेदनशील सूचना पनि आदानप्रदान भएको दाबी गरिएको छ। यस विषयमा आधिकारिक निष्कर्ष र थप विवरण सार्वजनिक हुन बाँकी छ।

जाँचबुझ प्रतिवेदनले दाहालको गतिविधि सशस्त्र प्रहरी नियमावली, २०७२ विपरीत देखिएको निष्कर्ष निकालेको बताइएको छ। अब प्रतिवेदनका आधारमा दाहालमाथि थप कारबाही गर्ने वा निलम्बन फुकुवा गर्ने भन्ने निर्णय गृह मन्त्रालयले गर्नेछ।

यसै प्रकरणमा सापकोटामाथि पनि प्रहरीले अनुसन्धान गरिरहेको छ। जबरालाई प्रहरी कार्यालयमा भेट्न गएको घटनासँगै सुरु भएको अनुसन्धानले उच्च सुरक्षा अधिकारी र अन्य व्यक्तिबीचको सम्पर्क तथा संवेदनशील सूचना आदानप्रदानबारे प्रश्न उठाएको छ।

५ हजार ७ सय मिटर उचाइमा सडक निर्माणको चुनौती! मुकोट हिमालको काखसम्म पुग्यो ६५ किलोमिटर सडक

अत्यन्तै कठिन हिमाली भूगोल र प्रतिकूल मौसमको चुनौती चिर्दै डोल्पाको मुकोट बस्ती सडक सञ्जालसँग जोडिएको छ। ठूली भेरी नदीको उद्गमस्थल मुकोट हिमालको काखसम्म सडक पुगेपछि वर्षौंदेखि विकटतामा रहेका स्थानीयको आवागमन सहज हुने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ।

छार्का ताङसोङ गाउँपालिकाका इन्जिनियर बमबहादुर भण्डारीका अनुसार मुस्ताङतर्फबाट गाउँपालिका–१ सम्म करिब ३० किलोमिटर र त्यहाँबाट मुकोटसम्म थप ३५ किलोमिटर गरी कुल करिब ६५ किलोमिटर सडक निर्माण गरिएको हो। यसमध्ये १० किलोमिटर सडक प्रदेश सरकारले र बाँकी गाउँपालिकाले निर्माण गरेको जनाइएको छ।

निर्माणका क्रममा हिउँ, अत्यधिक चिसो र कठिन भूगोलसँग जुध्नुपरेको थियो। सडक पुगेपछि स्थानीयलाई दैनिक उपभोग्य सामग्री ढुवानी, शिक्षा, स्वास्थ्य, व्यापार तथा पर्यटन प्रवर्द्धनमा सहजता हुने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ। मुस्ताङ हुँदै डोल्पा जोड्ने यस सडकले यात्राको दूरी घटाउनसमेत सहयोग पुग्ने विश्वास गरिएको छ।

एयरलाइन्सहरुको मनपरी बन्द, बालेनको निर्देशनपछि भाडा घटाउन सहमत भए एयरलाइन्स कम्पनी !

दसैँलगायत चाडपर्वमा हवाई टिकट महँगो भएको गुनासो बढेपछि प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाहको निर्देशनमा आन्तरिक वायुसेवा कम्पनीहरू स्वीकृत भाडादरभन्दा सस्तोमा टिकट बिक्री गर्न सहमत भएका छन्।

संस्कृति, पर्यटन तथा नागरिक उड्डयनमन्त्री खडकराज पौडेल (गणेश) को पहलमा नेपाल नागरिक उड्डयन प्राधिकरण (क्यान) ले बिहीबार वायुसेवा कम्पनीका प्रतिनिधिसँग छलफल गरेको थियो। छलफलमा सस्तो भाडादरमा टिकट बिक्री गर्ने र त्यसको विवरण सम्बन्धित कम्पनीका बिक्री प्लेटफर्ममा सार्वजनिक गर्ने सहमति भएको क्यानका महानिर्देशक मुकेश डङ्गोलले बताएका छन्। (गोरखापत्र)

चाडपर्वमा घर फर्किने यात्रुलाई राहत दिने उद्देश्यले अघि बढाइएको यो पहलले हवाई यात्राको खर्च घटाउन सहयोग पुग्ने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ। यद्यपि, सहमतिपछि सबै रुटको टिकट भाडा कति घट्छ भन्ने विवरण सार्वजनिक हुन बाँकी छ।

सूचनाका आधारमा गरिएको अपरेसनमा प्रहरीले तीन जना चिनियाँ नागरिकलाई पक्राउ गरेको हो। बरामद सुनको मूल्य त्यस दिनको बजार मूल्यअनुसार ५४ करोड ६० लाख ७ हजार ३२० रुपैयाँ रहेको प्रहरीले जनाएको छ।

काठमाडौं उपत्यका अपराध अनुसन्धान कार्यालयमा बुढानीलकण्ठ क्षेत्रमा चिनियाँ नागरिकले सुनको अवैध कारोबारका लागि कारखाना सञ्चालन गरिरहेको सूचना पुगेपछि प्रहरीले निगरानी र अनुसन्धान अघि बढाएको थियो। प्रारम्भिक रूपमा चार किलो सुन रहेको सूचना आए पनि छापा मार्दा त्यसको पाँच गुणाभन्दा बढी सुन फेला परेको कार्यालयले जनाएको छ।

प्रहरीले ‘अपरेसन ब्राभो गोल्फ’ नाम दिएर बुढानीलकण्ठ नगरपालिका–२, माथिल्लो भंगालस्थित घरमा छापा मारेको थियो। बिहीबार साँझ करिब ५ बजे पुगेको प्रहरी टोलीले पहिले नै निगरानी गरिएको घरलाई घेरा हालेर अपरेसन सञ्चालन गरेको थियो। घरको ढोका खोल्ने क्रममा चिनियाँ नागरिकसँग सामान्य धकेलाधकेलसमेत भएको प्रहरीले जनाएको छ।

छापाका क्रममा प्रहरीले सुनका टुक्रा, बिस्कुट आकारका ढिक्का, लेसिलो अवस्थामा रहेको सुन तथा धातुका टुक्रा बरामद गरेको थियो। घटनामा चीनका २७ वर्षीय हान फिई, ४७ वर्षीय चोउ लङसिन र ३७ वर्षीय वाङ जियान्जेन पक्राउ परेका छन्।

मासिक ३ लाख ३० हजार भाडामा घर लिएर सुन प्रशोधन

प्रहरीको प्रारम्भिक अनुसन्धानअनुसार सुन ल्याएर गाल्ने, विभिन्न आकारमा ढाल्ने र मागअनुसार बजारमा पठाउने उद्देश्यले घर भाडामा लिइएको थियो। उक्त घर चीनका नागरिक छु क्यानले मासिक तीन लाख ३० हजार रुपैयाँ भाडा तिर्ने गरी लिएको खुलेको छ।

प्रहरीका अनुसार छु क्यानले साउन ८ गते घरधनीसँग सम्झौता गरी चार महिनाको १३ लाख २० हजार रुपैयाँ भाडा अग्रिम भुक्तानी गरेका थिए। उनी अहिले अमेरिकामा बस्ने बिष्ट थरका व्यक्तिको घर भाडामा लिएर सुन प्रशोधनको व्यवस्था मिलाएपछि चीन फर्किएको अनुसन्धानमा खुलेको छ। अध्यागमनको अभिलेखअनुसार उनी साउन ३० गते चीन फर्किएका थिए र त्यसपछि नेपाल आएको देखिएको थिएन।

अनुसन्धान अधिकृतका अनुसार छु क्यानले घरको चाबी चीनमा रहेका जेन जिया लीलाई दिएका थिए। त्यसपछि जेन जिया लीले उक्त चाबी हान फिईलाई दिएर नेपाल पठाएको प्रारम्भिक अनुसन्धानमा देखिएको छ। हान फिईसहित तीन जना चिनियाँ नागरिकले उक्त घरमा सुन प्रशोधनको काम सञ्चालन गरेको प्रहरीको भनाइ छ।

सुन गालेर बिस्कुट बनाउने तयारी

प्रहरीको बुझाइमा भाडामा लिइएको घरको कम्पाउन्डभित्र सुन गाल्ने र विभिन्न आकारमा ढाल्ने उपकरण राखिएको थियो। नेपालमा सुनलाई लेसिलो अवस्थामा ल्याएर बाहिर प्लास्टिकले बेर्ने गरिएको हुन सक्ने प्रहरीको प्रारम्भिक आशंका छ। त्यसरी ल्याइएको सुनलाई ड्रायर मेसिनमा सुकाउने र त्यसपछि मेल्टिङ मेसिनमा पगालेर बिस्कुटलगायतका आकारमा ढाल्ने गरिएको हुन सक्ने अनुसन्धानबाट देखिएको प्रहरीले जनाएको छ।

तयार भएको सुन कहाँ र कसलाई बुझाउने भन्ने निर्देशन चीनमा रहेका व्यक्तिले दिने गरेको प्रहरीको प्रारम्भिक अनुसन्धानमा उल्लेख छ। पक्राउ परेका व्यक्तिहरूले चीनको ग्वान्जाओमा रहेका जेन जिया लीको निर्देशनमा काम गरेको बताएका छन्।

काठमाडौंमा सुन तयार भएपछि कहाँ पुर्‍याउने र कसलाई दिने भन्ने निर्देशन वी–च्याटमार्फत आउने गरेको प्रहरीको भनाइ छ। यद्यपि, सुनको अन्तिम गन्तव्य र कारोबारमा संलग्न अन्य व्यक्तिबारे अनुसन्धान जारी रहेको छ।

कारबाट पनि भेटियो दुई किलो सुन

प्रहरीले घरको कम्पाउन्डमा रहेको कारबाट एक–एक किलोका दुईवटा सुनका बिस्कुटसमेत बरामद गरेको छ। ती बिस्कुट कागजमा बेरेर चालक सिट नजिकको बक्समा राखिएको अवस्थामा फेला परेका थिए।

प्रहरीका अनुसार उक्त कार दैनिक आठ हजार रुपैयाँ भाडा तिर्ने गरी असोज ११ देखि २५ गतेसम्मका लागि लिइएको थियो। हान फिई असोज ११ गते काठमाडौं आएपछि कार भाडामा लिएको खुलेको छ।

कारमा तयारी अवस्थामा सुनका बिस्कुट भेटिएकाले बजारमा पुर्‍याउने तयारी भइरहेको हुन सक्ने प्रहरीको प्रारम्भिक विश्लेषण छ। तर उक्त सुन कहाँ लैजान लागिएको थियो भन्नेबारे अहिलेसम्म यकिन भइसकेको छैन।

चीनबाट निर्देशन आएको प्रहरीको आशंका

प्रहरीको प्रारम्भिक अनुसन्धानअनुसार काठमाडौंमा सञ्चालन गरिएको भनिएको सुन कारोबारको निर्देशन चीनमा रहेका व्यक्तिबाट आउने गरेको थियो। पक्राउ परेका हान फिईलाई उद्धृत गर्दै अनुसन्धान अधिकृतले ग्वान्जाओमा रहेका जेन जिया लीको निर्देशनअनुसार काम भएको देखिएको बताएका छन्।

प्रहरीका अनुसार छु क्यानले सुरुमा काठमाडौं आएर सुनको बजार र कारोबारको अवस्था बुझेका थिए। त्यसपछि घर भाडामा लिने तथा अन्य व्यवस्थापन मिलाएर चीन फर्किएको र पछि अर्को टोली नेपाल आएर काम अघि बढाएको हुन सक्ने अनुसन्धानमा देखिएको छ।

प्रहरीले चाडपर्वका बेला सुनको माग बढ्ने भएकाले नेपाली बजारमै बिक्री गर्ने उद्देश्यले कारोबार सञ्चालन गरिएको हुन सक्ने आशं

साउदी अरबको राजधानी रियादस्थित किङ खालिद अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय विमानस्थल र साउदी एयरलाइन्सको विमानलाई लक्षित गरी भएको आक्रमणमा विमानका कप्तानसहित तीन जनाको मृत्यु भएको छ। बिहीबार भएको आक्रमणमा विभिन्न देशका अन्य नागरिकसमेत घाइते भएका छन्।

शुक्रबार जारी हवाई सेवासम्बन्धी वक्तव्यअनुसार घाइतेहरूको अवस्था सामान्यदेखि गम्भीरसम्म रहेको छ। गत सप्ताहन्तदेखि यमनमा इरान समर्थित हुथी विद्रोहीविरुद्ध साउदी अरब र उसका सहयोगी सेनाले ठूलो सैन्य कारबाही सुरु गरेयता साउदी अरबमा भएको यो सबैभन्दा घातक आक्रमण भएको बताइएको छ।

साउदी अधिकारीहरूका अनुसार आक्रमणको पहिलो निशाना विमानस्थलका संरचना थिए भने दोस्रो आक्रमण साउदी एयरलाइन्सको विमानमा भएको थियो। आक्रमणमा संलग्न व्यक्तिको पहिचान सार्वजनिक गरिएको छैन। यद्यपि, हुथी विद्रोहीहरूले ब्यालेस्टिक क्षेप्यास्त्र प्रहार गरी विमानस्थललाई निशाना बनाएको दाबी गरेका छन्।

मृत्यु हुनेमध्ये साउदी एयरलाइन्सका कप्तान हमुद अली अलकलथामी पनि रहेको साउदी समूहले विज्ञप्तिमार्फत जनाएको छ। पछिल्लो सैन्य कारबाही सुरु भएयता साउदी राष्ट्रिय ध्वजावाहकको विमानमाथि भएको यो पहिलो पुष्टि भएको आक्रमण हो।

साउदी समूहका अनुसार आक्रमण हुँदा विमान जमिनमा रहेको थियो र त्यसमा क्षति पुगेको थियो। विमानमा भने कुनै यात्रु थिएनन्। रियादस्थित विमानस्थल पछिल्ला दिनमा पटकपटक आक्रमणको निशाना बन्दै आएको छ। यसै साताको सुरुमा भएको अर्को आक्रमणमा एक सुडानी नागरिकको मृत्यु भएको थियो।

आक्रमण भएको केही घण्टापछि बिहीबार साँझ ६ बजेदेखि विमानस्थलको सञ्चालन सामान्य अवस्थामा फर्किएको साउदी समूहले जनाएको छ।

यसैबीच, हुथी विद्रोहीविरुद्ध लडिरहेको साउदी नेतृत्वको गठबन्धनले क्षेत्रीय सुरक्षामा खतरा उत्पन्न गर्न विद्रोहीले प्रयोग गर्दै आएका तीनवटा रकेट प्रक्षेपण मञ्च नष्ट गरेको जनाएको छ।

यमनमा जारी सैन्य संघर्षका बीच साउदी अरबमा भएका पछिल्ला आक्रमणले क्षेत्रीय सुरक्षा अवस्था थप तनावपूर्ण बनेको छ।

खगेन्द्र सुनारलाई फिर्ता बोलाउन प्रधानमन्त्री बालेनलाई आफ्नै पार्टीबाट पत्र

 राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टी (रास्वपा) का सांसद खगेन्द्र सुनारलाई फिर्ता बोलाउन तथा उनीमाथि निष्पक्ष छानबिन गरी कारबाही गर्न माग गर्दै पार्टीकै एक सदस्यले प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन साहलाई पत्र पठाएका छन्।
